{{Short description|Stochastic process}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Dyson Brownian motion''' is a real-valued [[continuous-time]] [[stochastic process]] named for [[Freeman Dyson]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dyson |first=Freeman J. |date=1962-11-01 |title=A Brownian-Motion Model for the Eigenvalues of a Random Matrix |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/3/6/1191/228277/A-Brownian-Motion-Model-for-the-Eigenvalues-of-a |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=1191–1198 |doi=10.1063/1.1703862 |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Dyson studied this process in the context of [[Random matrix|random matrix theory]].

There are several equivalent definitions:<ref>{{Citation |chapter=Dyson Brownian Motion |date=2020 |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/first-course-in-random-matrix-theory/dyson-brownian-motion/F63EE7DFFF72FE3FD0A1B5B5F42818A2 |title=A First Course in Random Matrix Theory: for Physicists, Engineers and Data Scientists |pages=121–135 |editor-last=Bouchaud |editor-first=Jean-Philippe |access-date=2023-11-25 |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-48808-2 |editor2-last=Potters |editor2-first=Marc}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Tao |first=Terence |author-link=Terence Tao |date=2010-01-19 |title=254A, Notes 3b: Brownian motion and Dyson Brownian motion |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/01/18/254a-notes-3b-brownian-motion-and-dyson-brownian-motion/ |access-date=2023-11-25 |website=What's new |language=en}}</ref>

Definition by [[stochastic differential equation]]:<math display="block">d \lambda_i=d B_i+\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n: j \neq i} \frac{d t}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}</math>where <math>B_1, ..., B_n</math> are different and independent [[Wiener process]]es. Start with a [[Hermitian matrix]] with eigenvalues <math display="inline">\lambda_1(0), \lambda_2(0), ..., \lambda_n(0)</math>, then let it perform Brownian motion in the space of Hermitian matrices. Its eigenvalues constitute a Dyson Brownian motion. This is defined within the Weyl chamber <math>W_n := \{(x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \R^n: x_1 < \dots < x_n\}</math>, as well as any coordinate-permutation of it.

Start with <math display="inline">n</math> independent Wiener processes started at different locations <math display="inline">\lambda_1(0), \lambda_2(0), ..., \lambda_n(0)</math>, then condition on those processes to be non-intersecting for all time. The resulting process is a Dyson Brownian motion starting at the same <math display="inline">\lambda_1(0), \lambda_2(0), ..., \lambda_n(0)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Grabiner |first=David J. |date=1999 |title=Brownian motion in a Weyl chamber, non-colliding particles, and random matrices |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/?id=AIHPB_1999__35_2_177_0 |journal=Annales de l'I.H.P. Probabilités et statistiques |language=en |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=177–204 |issn=1778-7017}}</ref>

== Random matrix theory ==

In Random Matrix Theory, the Gaussian unitary ensemble is a fundamental ensemble. It is defined as a probability distribution over the space of <math display="inline">A \in \R^{n \times n}</math> [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian matrices]], with probability density function <math>\rho(A) \propto e^{- \frac 12 tr(A^2)}</math>.

Consider a Hermitian matrix <math display="inline">A \in \R^{n \times n}</math>. The space of Hermitian matrices can be mapped to the space of real vectors <math display="inline">\R^{n^2}</math>: <math display="block">
      A \mapsto (A_{11}, \dots, A_{nn}, \sqrt{2} Re(A_{12}), \dots, \sqrt{2} Re(A_{n-1, n}), \sqrt{2} Im(A_{12}), \dots, \sqrt{2} Im(A_{n-1, n}))
      </math>This is an isometry, where the matrix norm is [[Frobenius norm]]. By reversing this process, a standard Brownian motion in <math display="inline">\R^{n^2}</math> maps back to a Brownian motion in the space of <math display="inline">n\times n</math> Hermitian matrices:<math display="block">
        dA = \begin{bmatrix}
          dB_{11} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{12} + idB_{12}') & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{13} + idB_{13}') & \cdots & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{1n} + idB_{1n}') \\
          \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{12} - idB_{12}') & dB_{22} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{23} + idB_{23}') & \cdots & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{2n} + idB_{2n}') \\
          \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{13} - idB_{13}') & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{23} - idB_{23}') & dB_{33} & \cdots & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{3n} + idB_{3n}') \\
          \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
          \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{1n} - idB_{1n}') & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{2n} - idB_{2n}') & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (dB_{3n} - idB_{3n}') & \cdots & dB_{nn}
        \end{bmatrix}
        </math>The claim is that the eigenvalues of <math>A</math> evolve according to<ref name=":0" /><math display="block">d \lambda_i=d B_i+\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n: j \neq i} \frac{d t}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}</math>{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

Since each <math display="inline">dB</math> is on the order of <math display="inline">O(\sqrt{dt})</math>, we can equivalently write <math display="inline">dA = \sqrt{dt}G</math>, where <math display="inline">G</math> is a random Hermitian matrix where each entry is on the order of <math display="inline">O(1)</math>. By construction of the standard Brownian motion, <math display="inline">dA</math> is independent of <math display="inline">A</math>, so <math display="inline">G</math> is independent of <math display="inline">A</math>, and can be written as <math display="block">
        dA = \begin{bmatrix}
          X_{11} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{12} + iY_{12}) & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{13} + iY_{13}) & \cdots & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{1n} + iY_{1n}) \\
          \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{12} - iY_{12}) & X_{22} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{23} + iY_{23}) & \cdots & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{2n} + iY_{2n}) \\
          \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{13} - iY_{13}) & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{23} - iY_{23}) & X_{33} & \cdots & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{3n} + iY_{3n}) \\
          \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
          \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{1n} - iY_{1n}) & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{2n} - iY_{2n}) & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (X_{3n} - iY_{3n}) & \cdots & X_{nn}
        \end{bmatrix}
        </math> where each random variable <math display="inline">X_{ij}, Y_{ij}</math> is standard normal. In other words, <math display="inline">G</math> is distributed according to the [[gaussian unitary ensemble|GUE]](n).

By the first and second [[Hadamard variation formula]]s and Ito’s lemma, we have <math display="block">
      \lambda_i(t+dt) = \lambda_i(t) + \sqrt{dt} u_i^* G u_i + dt \sum_{j\neq i} \frac{\mathbb E[|u_i^* G u_j|^2]}{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}
      </math>

Since <math display="inline">G</math> is sampled from GUE(n), it is rotationally symmetric. Also, by assumption, the eigenvector <math display="inline">u_i</math> has norm 1, so <math display="inline">\sqrt{dt} u_i^* G u_i</math> has the same distribution as <math display="inline">\sqrt{dt} e_1^*G e_1</math>, which is distributed as <math display="inline">dB</math>.

Similarly, <math display="inline">\mathbb E[|u_i^* G u_j|^2] =1</math>.

}}{{hidden end}}

=== Infinitesimal generator ===
{{Main|Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)}}
Define the '''adjoint Dyson operator''':<math display="block">D^* F:=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \partial_{\lambda_i}^2 F+\sum_{1 \leq i, j \leq n: i \neq j} \frac{\partial_{\lambda_i} F}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j} .</math>For any smooth function <math>F: \R^n \to \R</math> with bounded derivatives, by direct differentiation, we have the [[Kolmogorov backward equations (diffusion)|Kolmogorov backward equation]] <math>\partial_t \mathbb E[F] = \mathbb E[D^* F] </math>. Therefore, the [[Kolmogorov Forward equation|Kolmogorov forward equation]] for the eigenspectrum is <math>\partial\rho = D\rho</math>, where <math>D</math> is the '''Dyson operator''' by<math display="block">D \rho:=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \partial_{\lambda_i}^2 \rho-\sum_{1 \leq i, j \leq n: i \neq j} \partial_{\lambda_i}\left(\frac{\rho}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}\right)</math>Let <math>\rho(t, \lambda) = \Delta_n(\lambda) u(t, \lambda)</math>, where <math>\Delta_n := \prod_{i < j}(\lambda_i - \lambda_j)</math> is the [[Vandermonde determinant]], then the time-evolution of eigenspectrum is equivalent to the time-evolution of <math>u</math>, which happens to satisfy the [[heat equation]] <math>\partial_t u = \frac 12 \sum_i \partial^2_i u</math>,

This can be proven by starting with the identity <math>\partial_{\lambda_i} \Delta_n= \Delta_n \sum_{1 \leq j \leq n: i \neq j} \frac{1}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}</math>, then apply the fact that the Vandermonde determinant is [[Harmonic function|harmonic]]: <math>\sum_i \partial_i^2 \Delta_n = 0</math>.

=== Johansson formula ===
Each Hermitian matrix with exactly two eigenvalues equal is [[Stabilizer subgroup|stabilized]] by <math>U(2) \times U(1)^{n-2}</math>, so its orbit under the action of <math>U(n)</math> has <math>\mathrm{dim}(U(n)) - \mathrm{dim}(U(2) \times U(1)^{n-2}) = n^2 - n - 2</math> dimensions. Since the space of <math>n-1</math> different eigenvalues is <math>(n-1)</math>-dimensional, the space of Hermitian matrix with exactly two eigenvalues equal has <math>n^2-3</math> dimensions.

By a dimension-counting argument, <math>\rho</math> vanishes at sufficiently high order on the border of the Weyl chamber, such that <math>u</math> can be extended to all of <math>\R^n</math> by antisymmetry, and this extension still satisfies the heat equation.

Now, suppose the random matrix walk begins at some deterministic <math>A(0)</math>. Let its eigenspectrum be <math>\nu = \lambda(A(0))</math>, then we have <math>u(0, \lambda) = \frac{1}{\Delta_n(\nu)} \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} (-1)^{|\sigma|} \delta(\lambda - \sigma(\nu))</math>, so by the solution to the heat equation, and the [[Leibniz formula for determinants]], we have<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johansson |first=Kurt Johansson |date=2001-01-01 |title=Universality of the local spacing distribution in certain ensembles of Hermitian Wigner matrices |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s002200000328 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=215 |issue=3 |pages=683–705 |doi=10.1007/s002200000328 |issn=1432-0916|arxiv=math-ph/0006020 }}</ref>

{{Math theorem|name=Johansson formula|note=|math_statement=

Let <math display="inline">A_0</math> be a Hermitian matrix with simple spectrum <math display="inline">\nu=\left(\nu_1, \ldots, \nu_n\right)</math>, let <math display="inline">t>0</math>, and let <math display="inline">A_t = A_0 + t^{1 / 2} G</math> where <math display="inline">G</math> is drawn from GUE. Then the spectrum <math display="inline">\lambda=\left(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\right)</math> of <math display="inline">A_t</math> has probability density function

<math display="block">
\rho(t, \lambda)=\frac{1}{(2 \pi t)^{n / 2}} \frac{\Delta_n(\lambda)}{\Delta_n(\nu)} \operatorname{det}\left(e^{-\left(\lambda_i-\nu_j\right)^2 / 2 t}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}
</math>

on the Weyl chamber.
}}

== Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber integral formula ==
Dyson Brownian motion allows a short proof of the [[Harish-Chandra]]-[[Claude Itzykson|Itzykson]]-[[Jean-Bernard Zuber|Zuber]] integral formula.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harish-Chandra |date=1957 |title=Differential Operators on a Semisimple Lie Algebra |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2372387 |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |volume=79 |issue=1 |pages=87–120 |doi=10.2307/2372387 |issn=0002-9327|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Itzykson |first=C. |last2=Zuber |first2=J.-B. |date=1980-03-01 |title=The planar approximation. II |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/21/3/411/225360/The-planar-approximation-II |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=411–421 |doi=10.1063/1.524438 |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tao |first=Terence |author-link=Terence Tao |date=2013-02-09 |title=The Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber integral formula |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2013/02/08/the-harish-chandra-itzykson-zuber-integral-formula/ |access-date=2025-01-30 |website=What's new |language=en}}</ref>

{{Math theorem
| name = Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber integral formula
| note = 
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">A, B</math> have no repeated eigenvalues, and <math display="inline">t</math> is a nonzero complex number, then - <math display="block">
      \int_{U(n)} \exp \left(t \operatorname{tr}\left(A U B U^*\right)\right) d U = c_n\frac{\det\left[\exp \left(t \lambda_i(A) \lambda_j(B)\right)\right]_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}}{t^{\left(n^2-n\right) / 2} \Delta_n(\lambda(A)) \Delta_n(\lambda(B))}
      </math>

where <math display="inline">U</math> is integrated over the Haar probability measure of the unitary group <math display="inline">U(n)</math>, and <math display="inline">c_n = \prod_{i=1}^{n} i!</math>.
}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

Let the GUE(n) probability distribution over <math display="inline">V_n</math> be defined as <math display="inline">\rho(M)dM</math>, where <math display="inline">dM = dM_{11}\dots dM_{nn}d(Re(M_{12})) \dots d(Im(M_{n, n-1}))</math>, and <math display="inline">\rho(M) = C_n e^{-\frac 12 tr(M^2)}</math> and <math display="inline">C_n</math> is a constant. Similarly, the eigenvalue distribution for the GUE(n) is <math display="block">\rho(\lambda) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{n / 2} c_n} \Delta_n(\lambda)^2 e^{-\|\lambda\|_2^2 / 2} d \lambda</math> where <math display="inline">d\lambda = d\lambda_1 \dots d\lambda_n</math>, and <math display="inline">c_n</math> is another constant., and <math display="inline">\Delta_n = \prod_{1 \leq i<j \leq n}\left(\lambda_i-\lambda_j\right)</math> is the Vandermonde determinant.

If <math display="inline">f: V_n \to \C</math> is unitarily invariant, with sufficient regularity and decay, then it can be decomposed as <math display="inline">f(M_n) = f(\lambda(M_n))</math>. By Riesz representation theorem, there exists some function <math display="inline">w</math> such that <math display="inline">\int f(M) dM = \int f(\lambda) w(\lambda) d\lambda</math>, which by the above argument equals <math display="block">
      w(\lambda) = \rho(\lambda) / \rho(M) =  \frac{\Delta_n(\lambda)^2}{c_nC_n (2\pi)^{n/2}}
      </math>
	  
Given two such unitarily invariant functions <math display="inline">f, g</math> with sufficient regularity and decay, then consider their heat kernel convolution <math display="block">
      X = \iint dAdB \; f(A) \frac{C_n}{t^{n^2/2}}e^{-\frac{tr(A-B)^2}{2t}}g(B)
      </math>
	  
We compute <math display="inline">X</math> in one way.

Let <math display="inline">f_t(A) := f(A) e^{-\frac{tr(A^2)}{2t}}, g_t(B) := g(B) e^{-\frac{tr(B^2)}{2t}}</math>, then the quantity is <math display="block">
          \begin{aligned}
          X&=  \frac{C_n}{t^{n^2/2}} \int_{V_n}\int_{V_n} f_t(A) e^{-\frac{tr(AB)}{t}} g_t(B) dAdB \\
          &=  \frac{C_n}{t^{n^2/2}} \int_{V_n}\int_{V_n}\int_{U(n)} f_t(A) e^{\frac{tr(AUBU^*)}{t}} g_t(B) dAdBdU \\
          &=  \frac{C_n}{t^{n^2/2}} \int_{V_n}\int_{V_n} f_t(A) K_t(A,B) g_t(B) dAdB\\
          \end{aligned}
          </math> where we integrate over the Haar measure of the unitary group <math display="inline">U(n)</math>, and use the fact that <math display="inline">g_t(B)</math> is unitarily invariant, and we define the kernel<br />
<math display="block">
          K_t(A,B) := \int_{U(n)}e^{\frac{tr(AUBU^*)}{t}} dU
          </math>

Since <math display="inline">K_t, f_t, g_t</math> are all unitarily invariant, we have <math display="block">
          X = \frac{1}{C_n(2 \pi)^n c_n^2 t^{n^2 / 2}} \int_{W_n} \int_{W_n} f_t(\lambda) g_t(\nu) K_t(\lambda, \nu) \Delta_n(\lambda)^2 \Delta_n(\nu)^2 d \lambda d \nu
          </math>

We compute <math display="inline">X</math> in another way.

Fix <math display="inline">B</math>, then set <math display="inline">G = (A-B)/\sqrt t</math>, then we have <math display="block">
          X = \int_{V_n}\int_{V_n} f(B+\sqrt{t}G)C_n e^{-\frac 12 tr(G^2)}  dGdB
          </math>

Apply the Johansson formula, and convert the domain of integral to the Weyl chamber: <math display="block">
          X = \frac{1}{C_nc_n(2\pi)^{n}t^{n/2}}\iint f(\lambda) g(\nu) \Delta_n(\lambda) \Delta_n(\nu) \det\left[e^{-\frac{(\lambda_i - \nu_j)^2}{2t}}\right]_{i,j} d\lambda d\nu 
          </math>
		  
Equate the two results, and simplify, we obtain the equality.

}}{{hidden end}}

== Ginibre formula ==
{{Math theorem
| name = Ginibre formula
| note = Tao 2012, page 251
| math_statement = <math display="block">
      \rho(\lambda)=\frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{n / 2} 1!\ldots n!} e^{-|\lambda|^2 / 2}\left|\Delta_n(\lambda)\right|^2
      </math>
on the Weyl chamber.
}}
	  {{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

The GUE is constructed as the <math display="inline">t=1</math> distribution when starting with <math display="inline">A_0</math>. So we take <math display="inline">t=1</math> and <math display="inline">\nu \to 0</math> in the Johansson formula.

<math display="block">
      \rho(\lambda)= \frac{\Delta_n(\lambda)}{(2 \pi)^{n / 2}}  \lim_{\nu \to 0}\frac{1}{\Delta_n(\nu)} \operatorname{det}\left(e^{-\frac 12 \left(\lambda_i-\nu_j\right)^2}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}
      </math>
	  
	  Since <math display="inline">e^{-\left(\lambda_i-\nu_j\right)^2 / 2} = e^{-\lambda_i^2/2}e^{-\nu_j^2/2}e^{\lambda_i \nu_j}</math>, we have <math display="block">
      \operatorname{det}\left(e^{-\left(\lambda_i-\nu_j\right)^2 / 2}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}=e^{-|\lambda|^2 / 2} e^{-|\nu|^2 / 2} \operatorname{det}\left(e^{\lambda_i \nu_j}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}
      </math>
	  
	  Now by a property of [[Vandermonde matrix#Generalizations|Vandermonde matrix]], at the <math display="inline">\nu \to 0</math> limit,

<math display="block">
      \operatorname{det}\left(e^{\lambda_i \nu_j}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}=\frac{1}{1!\ldots n!} \Delta_n(\lambda) \Delta_n(\nu)+o\left(\Delta_n(\nu)\right)
      </math>
uniformly in <math display="inline">\nu</math>.
	  }}{{hidden end}}
